column5: Prayer begins with Father and holy name
column6: Jesus' prayer addresses the Father and asks that his name be hallowed, adding Luke's distinct liturgical form to the Fatiha's named invocation and direct address.

column5: Daily bread as dependence
column6: The prayer asks for daily bread, giving a concrete petition for provision within the same short prayer that asks for God's reign.

column5: Forgiveness and protection from misdirection
column6: The prayer asks forgiveness and not to be brought into trial, a distinct compact counterpart to the Fatiha's dependence, guidance, and avoidance of failed paths.

column5: Wanderers cannot find a way to an inhabited city
column6: The psalm describes hungry and thirsty travelers lost in a wilderness with no city in reach, closely meeting the commentary's lost traveler and destination-home imagery.

column5: The lost cry to YHWH for help
column6: The wanderers cry to God in distress and he rescues them, matching the commentary's needy traveler who asks the Lord for aid.

column5: God leads them by a straight way to a city
column6: YHWH guides the travelers on a straight road to an inhabited city, joining the commentary's requested guidance, straight path, and arrival place in one scene.

column5: Thanks for steadfast love after rescue
column6: The rescued are urged to thank YHWH for his steadfast love, linking praise to the help received along the road.

column5: God satisfies the thirsty and hungry
column6: God fills the hungry and satisfies the thirsty, adding provision to the lost traveler's rescue and the commentary's water imagery.

column5: A highway called the holy way
column6: Isaiah describes a raised road for the redeemed, called the Way of Holiness, giving a communal and sacred version of the straight path requested in the Fatiha.

column5: No danger on the redeemed road
column6: No lion or dangerous beast is found on this highway, a concrete promise of safe travel for the people whom God guides.

column5: The redeemed return to Zion with joy
column6: The travelers arrive in Zion singing, with lasting joy, giving the commentary's road a communal destination in God's house.

column5: God leads exiles by streams of water on a straight path
column6: Jeremiah pictures God guiding returning Israel beside streams and on a straight road, while calling Israel God's firstborn; this joins the commentary's water, way, and belonging-to-the-Lord images.

column5: Prepare a road for YHWH in the wilderness
column6: The voice calls for a road to be made straight in the wilderness, matching the commentary's image of a path prepared by others for the guided traveler.

column5: The road is leveled for the coming Lord
column6: Valleys rise and rough ground is leveled, making straightness physical and communal as in the commentary's trodden, smoothed road.

column5: Mark applies Isaiah's road to John's preparation
column6: Mark identifies Isaiah's wilderness voice with John the Baptist preparing the Lord's way; this Christian reading makes the straight road a call to prepare for God's arrival.

column5: Show me the way I should walk
column6: The speaker asks God to let him hear steadfast love and show the way to go, closely joining the Fatiha's request for guidance with its reliance on mercy.

column5: God's good spirit leads on level ground
column6: The psalm asks God's spirit to lead the speaker on level ground, a direct image of the upright path and guide developed in the commentary.

column5: The Lord is gracious, compassionate, and slow to anger
column6: This praise formula names the same divine qualities as the Fatiha's mercy names and places them within a hymn of praise.

column5: The Lord's compassion extends to all he made
column6: God's compassion reaches all his works, concretely joining mercy to the commentary's Lord of all worlds.

column5: God's kingdom is everlasting and faithful
column6: The psalm's account of God's enduring kingdom joins praise of divine sovereignty to the commentary's master of the judgment day.

column5: All creatures look to God for food
column6: Every living thing looks to God for sustenance, matching the commentary's picture of the needy traveler and its Lord who provides.

column5: God opens his hand and satisfies living things
column6: The open hand that satisfies all living things gives a specific image for completed divine favor and care.

column5: The blessed person meditates on Torah day and night
column6: The psalm defines the blessed person's way through delight in God's instruction, adding a Torah-centered Jewish account of how the favored path is walked.

column5: The righteous are planted beside water
column6: The person on the good way is like a tree planted beside streams, bearing fruit in season; this links the blessed path to the commentary's water and nourishment imagery.

column5: Walking God's way is imitation of God's traits
column6: The midrash reads “walk in all his ways” as imitating God's compassion and other attributes; it turns the commentary's literal path joined to worship into an ethical practice of mercy.

column5: The Father's house has many dwellings
column6: Jesus speaks of dwelling places in his Father's house, giving a specific Christian destination-house image for the commentary's road toward a home.

column5: The guide brings his followers to the house
column6: Jesus promises to return and take his followers to himself, connecting a trusted guide with arrival at the Father's house.

column5: The disciples are shown the way to the destination
column6: Jesus says the disciples know the way to where he is going, a direct meeting of guide, road, and destination.

column5: Jesus identifies himself as the way to the Father
column6: Jesus calls himself the way and says access to the Father is through him, a Christian interpretation that makes the requested path personal and relational.

column5: God's mercy brings dawn to those in darkness
column6: Zechariah's song says God's tender mercy brings light to those sitting in darkness, joining mercy with the commentary's lostness and its contrast between radiant and dark outcomes.

column5: God guides feet into the way of peace
column6: The song says the dawn will guide people's feet into the way of peace, closely matching the Fatiha's request for a straight path and the commentary's walking image.

column5: The fallen opponents contrast with those who rise and stand
column6: The psalm says others collapse and fall while the worshippers rise and stand, closely matching the commentary's contrast between falling under wrath and upright walking.

column5: The day is wrath, distress, and devastation
column6: Zephaniah calls YHWH's day a day of wrath and distress, giving the commentary's judgment day a sharply adverse side.

column5: The day brings alarm against fortified cities
column6: The trumpet and alarm on that day give a specific public scene of judgment rather than a generic reference to divine anger.

column5: The day consumes the earth in divine anger
column6: The oracle says neither silver nor gold can rescue people from YHWH's wrath, adding a concrete reckoning to the commentary's account of judgment.

column5: A creditor must respect the debtor's household
column6: The creditor may not enter the borrower's house to seize a pledge, a concrete legal limit on the debt relation behind the commentary's debt and witness imagery.

column5: The borrower brings the pledge out
column6: The lender must remain outside while the debtor brings the pledge, preserving the debtor's agency within the written obligation.

column5: A poor debtor's cloak cannot be kept overnight
column6: The creditor must not retain a poor person's pledge, directly connecting debt law with care for a vulnerable person.

column5: Returning the cloak is righteousness before God
column6: The pledge must be returned before sunset so the debtor can sleep in it; God hears the debtor's cry, joining debt, timely repayment, and divine judgment of conduct.

column5: A king settles accounts with his servants
column6: Jesus begins a parable with a king who calls servants to settle their debts, bringing the commentary's king, day of repayment, and debt together in one scene.

column5: A servant owes an unpayable sum
column6: The first servant's vast debt makes the account concrete and sets up the king's decision about repayment and mercy.

column5: The debtor asks for patience
column6: The servant falls down and asks the king for patience, matching the commentary's dependent petitioner before a sovereign.

column5: The king releases the debt out of compassion
column6: The king has compassion and cancels the debt, combining sovereignty, repayment, and mercy in a direct parallel to the commentary's divine attributes.

column5: The forgiven servant demands payment from another
column6: The servant then seizes a fellow servant over a smaller debt, turning received mercy into a test of how the forgiven person treats others.

column5: The king recalls the canceled debt
column6: The king confronts the servant with the debt he had canceled, making remembered mercy and account-keeping central to judgment.

column5: The servant should have shown compassion
column6: The king asks whether the servant should have shown the same mercy he received, connecting compassion to the ethical use of favor.

column5: The king hands the unmerciful debtor over
column6: The angry king delivers the servant to punishment until the debt is paid, directly joining unpaid debt, wrath, and reckoning.

column5: The parable applies the account to forgiveness
column6: Jesus says the heavenly Father will treat those who refuse forgiveness similarly, making mercy the decisive conduct at the final account.

column5: Forgive a neighbor and one's own sins are forgiven
column6: Sirach directly joins forgiving another's wrong with forgiveness when one prays, adding a Jewish ethical interpretation to the commentary's pairing of mercy and judgment.

column5: The written debt record is erased
column6: Paul says the record of debt against people is canceled and removed, a Christian theological reading that turns the commentary's written account into an image of forgiven guilt.

column5: The weary are invited to come for rest
column6: Jesus invites the weary and burdened to come to him for rest, matching the commentary's tired traveler who asks for help.

column5: A gentle teacher gives a yoke
column6: Jesus calls disciples to take his yoke and learn from him because he is gentle and humble; as a discipleship metaphor, it connects the commentary's voluntarily tamed servant with rest under a trusted guide.

column5: The teacher's yoke is easy
column6: Jesus says his yoke is easy and burden light, giving a concrete contrast to coercive enslavement in the commentary's Moses scene.

column5: God leads the blind by an unknown road
column6: YHWH promises to lead the blind on an unfamiliar path and turn darkness to light, directly joining lostness, guidance, and divine care.

column5: The guide does not abandon those he leads
column6: The same promise says God will not forsake them, contrasting the commentary's unrecognized owner with a Lord who remains responsible for the lost.

column5: The traveler bows after God guides him
column6: Abraham's servant bows and worships YHWH at the well after seeing the sign, adding an explicit worship response to the commentary's meeting of guidance, water, and travel.

column5: Two people go to the temple to pray
column6: Jesus frames the contrast as a temple encounter, giving a concrete communal setting to the commentary's worshipper speaking directly to God.

column5: The tax collector asks God for mercy without lifting his eyes
column6: The petitioner stands at a distance and asks for mercy, a specific posture of dependence that echoes the commentary's needy servant asking the Lord for help.

column5: The humble petitioner goes home justified
column6: Jesus says the humble petitioner, rather than the self-exalting one, is justified; this joins prayer, moral standing, and the final verdict.
